reasons: The lake identity record verifies Wilson v. Layne as a U.S. Supreme Court case decided 1999-05-24, with year 1999.
The lake citation record lists official citation 526 U.S. 603, parallel citations 119 S. Ct. 1692 and 143 L. Ed. 2d 818, and vendor-neutral citation 1999 U.S. LEXIS 3633.
The opinion analyzes whether media presence during execution of a home warrant exceeded the authorized intrusion.
The opinion states that police actions in execution of a warrant must be related to the objectives of the authorized intrusion, supporting placement under scope/manner issues.
The opinion expressly applies qualified-immunity doctrine and the Harlow clearly-established standard.
The holding grants qualified immunity because the right was not clearly established at the time; the lake progeny record also reflects substantial later citation activity.
residual_risks: The exact taxonomy label 'Key — Progeny / Refinement' is editorial, but the disclosed record supports the qualified-immunity home role.

reasons: The text at page 614 states that bringing media or other third parties into a home during warrant execution violates the Fourth Amendment when their presence is not in aid of executing the warrant.
The opening paragraph and qualified-immunity discussion state that officers were entitled to qualified immunity because the law was not clearly established when the search occurred.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: For maximum precision, 'when not in aid of the warrant' could be phrased as 'when not in aid of the execution of the warrant.'
